title: When Not to Automate — Module Quiz

items.q: What is the first question to ask of a task you are thinking of automating?
options: How much time would it save?
What is this work for, beyond its output?
Which tool is cheapest?
items.explain: If the answer is only the output, automate with care. If it includes what the work does to the people involved, slow down.

items.q: What is protective friction?
options: A slow tool that frustrates users
A deliberate slowness or extra step that exists to prevent harm, such as a second approval or a waiting period
The cost of switching vendors
items.explain: Removing it for efficiency removes the protection too. The giveaway is that people complain and nobody remembers why it was there. Find out first.

items.q: Why is a task done three times a year a poor candidate for automation?
options: Rare tasks are easier to do by hand
Automation pays back through repetition, and one that runs rarely will have rotted between runs
Rare tasks are not important
items.explain: The cost of building, testing and keeping it exceeds the saving, and the manual version stays fresh by being used.

items.q: Why should a decision about whether to hire someone not be made by a tool alone?
options: Tools are not allowed to process applications
The decision must be one a person can make, justify and own, and if the tool decides, the thing that gave it legitimacy has gone
Tools are slower than people at reading applications
items.explain: A tool can inform the decision. Where why did you decide that must have a human answer, the human has to decide.

items.q: Why does automating a flawed process make the flaws harder to change?
options: Automated processes cannot be edited
A manual process is adjusted by telling people, while an automated one needs someone to find and alter the code, so the fault becomes infrastructure
Automation hides the flaws from view
items.explain: Fixing a process is cheapest before anything is built on it.

items.q: How do you test whether a process is ready to be automated?
options: Check whether a vendor offers a template for it
Ask whether a new colleague could do it correctly from the written steps alone
Count how many people currently do it
items.explain: If not, either the steps are unwritten or the work depends on knowledge nobody has recorded, and you cannot yet tell an automation what to do.

items.q: What does a high share of exceptions tell you about a process?
options: The staff are poorly trained
The official process describes the easy cases, and an automation built from it will handle only those
The process is ready to automate
items.explain: Each exception is a trace of something the official process did not anticipate, and often a clue to what the process is really for.

items.q: A step in a process exists and nobody knows why. What should you do before deleting it?
options: Delete it immediately to save time
Find out why it exists, since it may be a protection, by asking whoever has been there longest
Automate it as it stands
items.explain: Deleting a step whose purpose you do not understand is how protections disappear.

items.q: How can an automation go wrong by working well?
options: It becomes too fast for people to follow
People stop doing the task by hand, so the skill and knowledge fade just as the automation becomes the only way the work gets done
It generates more work than staff can handle
items.explain: A dependence nobody chose appears. Then the automation fails and the manual path is needed by people who have never used it.

items.q: Why might a reviewer of drafted work eventually be unable to review it?
options: Reviewers are paid less than writers
Judging whether output is subtly wrong comes from having done the work, which the automation now does for them
Drafts become too long to read
items.explain: Keep people doing enough of the underlying work, and enough independent checking, that the judgement survives.

items.q: What is the best way to keep a manual capability alive?
options: Write a procedure once and file it
Run it by hand on a schedule, rotate who does it, and treat each run as a test of the fallback
Hire a specialist for emergencies
items.explain: Every manual run is a test of the procedure. Where it was wrong or missing something, fix it then.

items.q: Why is 'the system decided' not an acceptable answer to the person affected?
options: Systems are often wrong
A system cannot be asked, held responsible or put right; someone chose to build and rely on it, and that person owes an answer
It is forbidden by every privacy law
items.explain: The affected person is owed an answer from a human who can explain, reconsider and put it right.

items.q: What makes an appeal route against an automated decision genuine?
options: It is documented in a policy page
A person looks at it, with the information and the authority to disagree with the system
It is handled by the same automation to ensure consistency
items.explain: An appeal route that goes back to the same automation is a loop, and a human who can only confirm the output is a rubber stamp.

items.q: Why should the record behind an automated decision be written by your own code?
options: Models cannot produce logs
A person asked to explain a decision needs a reconstructable record, not memory or guesswork
Records are cheaper when automated
items.explain: Record the input, what it did, what it decided, when and which version. Hold it with minimal content and a defined retention, as P8 explains.

items.q: What is the simplest test of whether an automation treats the people it affects fairly?
options: Whether it saves more than it costs
Whether they would be comfortable knowing exactly what is happening
Whether it complies with the vendor's terms
items.explain: If not, change what you do or tell them and see what they say. Carrying on in the hope they will not find out costs far more than honesty would have.

items.q: Why does the duty of care rise for people who cannot easily walk away?
options: They are more likely to complain
The usual protection of choosing elsewhere does not apply, so the only protection is what you build in
Regulators inspect those services more often
items.explain: Patients, applicants, children and the dependent are protected by disclosure, a human route and restraint about what is automated.

items.q: Why can an automation without a human alternative be exclusionary?
options: Humans are always faster
Some people cannot use the automated route, through connection, confidence, disability or language
Regulators require a human alternative everywhere
items.explain: It is a cost you impose without seeing it. A real, findable human route need not be instant to change how the interaction feels.

items.q: Why is a stop control tested only against an already-broken system worthless?
options: Broken systems ignore stop commands
Stopped and already broken look identical, so the test reports success either way
The control needs live traffic to initialise
items.explain: The observation that means something is: running, press it, confirm it stops.

items.q: Why must a stop control come with a manual path?
options: Regulators require one
Stopping an automation without a way to do the work just turns a malfunction into an outage
Manual paths are cheaper to run
items.explain: Write the procedure, have a person who can run it, and tell affected people what to do instead.

items.q: Why is disabling a workflow without revoking its connection an incomplete retirement?
options: Disabled workflows are still billed
The credential stays live with no owner or purpose, a standing grant waiting to be misused
The platform re-enables it after a month
items.explain: Revoke at the service itself, delete or archive the credentials, update the inventory and tell the people who relied on it.

items.q: Why is 'it works' not a sufficient reason to switch a feature on?
options: Working code is rarely stable
Technical success and readiness differ: people, safeguards, measurements and consent can be missing while the code is flawless
Launching later always produces a better product
items.explain: The missing piece is around the feature, not in it. For features touching children, money or safety, the cost of launching early is paid by others.

items.q: What is a conjunctive gate?
options: A gate controlled by two administrators
A condition requiring several things to be true at once, so no single flag can open it alone
A gate that opens automatically after a deadline
items.explain: Certification opens only if the switch is on and two different reviewers exist and have agreed and the other conditions hold. Remove any one and it stays shut.

items.q: A launch condition is enforced only by a disabled button in the interface. What is it?
options: A strong control, because users cannot click it
A hint, since the layer behind the button does not check it
A legal requirement
items.explain: A safeguard is only as real as the layer that enforces it. Put the condition in the database function or server code that cannot be bypassed.

items.q: Why write the conditions for opening a feature before the pressure to launch arrives?
options: Regulators require written conditions
A condition written after the fact bends to fit what is convenient, while one written beforehand does not
It speeds up the launch
items.explain: Make each condition specific enough to check. When confident is not a condition; two reviewers have each recorded agreement on twenty sample answers is.

items.q: Why should 'do nothing' appear among the alternatives on a decision record?
options: It satisfies a formal requirement
It is often the right answer and is rarely written down; if you cannot say why it is worse, you have not justified building
It shows the decision was taken carefully
items.explain: Sometimes the process is tolerable and the build would cost more than it saves.

items.q: Why write the decision record before building rather than afterwards?
options: Records written afterwards are rejected by regulators
After the work is done the rationale drifts to justify what was built, and writing it first changes decisions
It is quicker to write before the details are known
items.explain: Writing what could go wrong often reveals something that cannot be repaired, and writing do-nothing sometimes shows the problem was smaller than the solution.

items.q: What is the right amount of automation?
options: As much as the tools make possible
Often less than is possible, since every automation is a commitment to own, watch, keep true and retire
Whatever saves the most time
items.explain: Make commitments where the return is worth it. The judgement about what to build and what to leave is the skill that does not age when the tools change.

items.q: In what position is a person who is on the receiving end of an automated decision and cannot reach a human?
options: Protected by the system's accuracy
Stuck, since an appeal route that loops back to the same automation is not a route
Able to demand a refund
items.explain: Give affected people a clear, findable way to reach a person who can genuinely reconsider, and a realistic timescale that you meet.
